utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I do understand that the Prosecution wanted to raise a brief -- the Defence wanted to raise a brief matter. I'm looking in your direction, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes. We read one portion of the document, P6966, on Tuesday with the redirect of our Witness Milojica, and we would kindly ask for that portion to be translated and included into already admitted document. I raised the issue this morning with Mr. Traldi, but since he was not at that time with the witness, I expect him not to have ready answer. So I just kindly ask him to consult with his colleagues what is the position of Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We are in the process of doing that, and we'll get back to Mr. Lukic promptly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the Chamber even asked for more background to see whether there was more known about what the statement of the witness exactly had been which resulted in certain conclusions by the Chamber in that judgement. So, therefore, it's -- the Chamber always agrees that if the parties are of the same opinion, then that's fine; but then if Mr. Zec would in this case not agree, then the Chamber may also consider its own position in this respect and may ask for further portions. But I can imagine that the parties want to acquaint themselves with the documentation in its entirety before they make a choice. And, in that respect, it's appreciated, Mr. Lukic, that a continuing conversation between the parties may lead to the best results. That's on the record. And the witness may already be escorted into the courtroom. I meanwhile deal briefly with a matter related to -- it's Exhibit D758. D758 was admitted through Witness Puhalac, and on the 10th of November, the statement was admitted into evidence under number D758. Following the discovery of some translation errors, the Defence requested a verification of the translation, and the Chamber was informed yesterday through an informal communication that a new CLSS translation was uploaded in e-court under doc ID number 1D19-0605. And Madam Registrar is hereby instructed to replace the previous translation in e-court with the revised one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, as always, the other party in this case, the Prosecution, has an opportunity to revisit the matter within the next 48 hours. Good morning, Mr. Krsic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And Mr. Lukic will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Krsic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we have a lot of topics to go through, I just wanted to ask you to try to give shorter answers, please. In paragraphs 7 to 20 of your statement, in the bulk of your statement you speak about the incident in Grabovica. Just briefly, could you please look at paragraph 7. To whom did these people surrender? How did it come about that they surrendered? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people surrendered to our unit, parts of the Grabovac Company, which was deployed in the area of Duboka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now paragraph 8. In the second sentence of paragraph 8, you say: "Commander Novakovic ordered me to organise the reception of weapons, and then I collected 35 to 40 pieces of weaponry of different calibre." How was the weaponry brought in front of the Grabovica school?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons were brought by our soldiers who were from the Grabovica Company and were deployed in the Duboka sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you help me? I tried to find your -- the sentence you have read into the transcript. I read: "Commander Novakovic asked me to organise the collection of weapons ..." I find that, but I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps -- it's the second sentence of paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you. I missed that. But while I have the floor, I would like to ask the witness. You are talking in paragraph 7 and the following paragraphs about the incident in the Grabovica school. Can you tell me when took this incident place? What is the date of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, the incident happened on the 3rd and 4th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you were receiving the weapons, what was going on during that time that you were busy with the weapons?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and the platoon commander, Bosko Djuric, from the Grabovica Company were receiving the weapons. We had a small truck which was a little bit farther away from the football pitch, and then the soldiers were coming in turns and bringing the weapons. We had time to see that the commander when he was managing the situation, he made -- he organised it so that people were being taken to the school in groups. People were being taken to the school in groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph in the English version --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version, sixth line from the top, and in the B/C/S version it's the fifth line from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it states -- it's a full sentence: "After accommodating the personnel, Novakovic ordered me to stay in Grabovica to make a list of the people and to deliver this list to him the next morning." Could you please tell us who were you putting down on that list first and where?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I finished all my earlier set tasks about the security, I set off to carry out the tasks set to me by the commander, and then first I listed all the women and children who were in the classroom on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where were you when this list was being made?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the classroom where the women and children were. And as far as I can remember, I wrote down the names of 30 to 40 women. Why do I remember this number, more or less? There are a number of reasons for that. First of all, I could see in front of me this group, that's one thing. Secondly, they were placed in a classroom, and according to the principle of logical conclusion, our classrooms could accommodate between 30 to 40 pupils. And some of those seats, when the women and children were sitting down, were not filled. So the only possible thing was to conclude that the number of the people there was between 30 and 40. I went for the higher number because usually teaching groups, groups of pupils on average number 30 people. They could be larger, but as I said, I picked the higher figure, between 30 to 40 people. And this is something that applies to most schools. There wouldn't be any more people, particularly not in elementary schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who did you compile a list of after you compiled a list of the women?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I compiled a list of the women and children, I went out of the classroom. I went upstairs to the first floor because there were more classrooms on the first floor and the men were placed in some of those classrooms. Somebody who was with me suggested that we compile the list in an empty classroom, that men would be brought in in twos or three threes, so I agreed to that. I went to the last classroom in line, I sat down at the teacher's desk, there were two policemen with me, and they were bringing in two or three men at a time who sat in front of me. And that is how I took down their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, what did you write down? What did you ask them?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main information that I took from them was their first and last name, date of birth, and the place they were from, or their place of residence. I did not take any other information or interview them or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the men who were brought before you, did you notice if any of them were beaten, did they have bruises, were they bleeding?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. The people who were in front of me were sitting like this. They were sitting right in front of me, perhaps half a metre away from the desk at which I was sitting. They would place their hands on the desk, taking up a position that I am taking up now. Perhaps they were leaning a little bit forward. So that's how they were sitting. They were so close to me that it was impossible that I did not notice anything if they had anything -- any marks on their face.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next question: From the point in time when those Muslims came to the school playing field in Grabovica to the moment that you left Grabovica, did you notice whether any of those men were tied with anything, ropes or any other kind of ligatures?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely no. When they came to the football pitch, from that area, they were brought to the school and placed into classrooms. No actions were applied that would violate the dignity of those people, violate human dignity; i.e., nothing was done that could possibly be done when we're talking about actions of the police or anything else. Something else that I could say about this: During the preparation earlier, I listened to the testimony of one witness of the Prosecution, I think he was one of the first victims -- witnesses. I don't know his name --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Don't mention his name.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So this witness who as a child was present during the events in Grabovica, he said that he saw that those men were tied with wire. This is absolutely incorrect. First of all, he said that as a child he noticed that the commander had something shiny above his head. Actually, when those people were brought, it was already dark. Commander Novakovic was holding a light above his head, and he was shedding light at the people who were in the playground. So it's true that there was something shiny above his head. So if the commander at that point in time had a torch so that he could have some light for those people, it means that it was difficult to notice the actual people. So can you imagine that in such darkness you would be able to see that those people were -- had their hands tied with wire? To me, that's incomprehensible. And I state with full responsibility, I guarantee that with my life, that while I was in Grabovica, those people were not tied with anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While the commander was casting this light from the torch to the people, would it then be impossible to see where the light is going, whether a person is tied with ligature or not? I'm sure that it would be possible, wouldn't it be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was possible to see with a torch if some of those people were tied or not, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was it that you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to add that those people were received in Duboka and they arrived in a column. I was there when they arrived in that column, and they were not tied. I saw that myself. It's true that it's quite dark, but I was able to see. People were moving their hands. As they were walking, they were moving their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 20, 21, and 22, you say -- you talk about what you did when you left Grabovica. Did you ever find out what happened in Grabovica on that occasion once you left? Are you able to tell us what you found out, how did you find out, from whom? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left Grabovica, there were these activities, but the first news I heard in relation to Grabovica was when I was touring one of the companies and some of the soldiers were asking questions about what happened in Grabovica. I said that there were problems, because I was present when one of those problems occurred, and that I didn't know about what happened later. And then they told me that there was chaos there. I told them I didn't have any information about it. And then once I returned to the command, sometime - I don't know whether it was two or three days later - that was when I found out about it for the first time. The commander's assistant for security, Major Mirko Bosic, entered my office, and he -- well, when he entered my office, I asked him, Mirko, what happened up there in Grabovica? And he literally said to me, "Vojkan" -- I apologise for using this term. I will try to interpret what he said. So he said "Vojkane, fuck it. There were some problems. The population in Grabovica fucked up the situation and people were killed." That is what he told me. I was surprised to say the least. And then he also told me -- I was in a state of shock, and then he used that opportunity and added: Listen, I have come here so that you could write a statement. The command of the 1st Krajina Corps is asking for statements regarding the events in Grabovica. He gave me instructions. He told me that I should write a statement for the period that I was there about what was going on in Grabovica. I wrote the statement and I handed it to him. I also want to add here that in the statement what is written there is more or less the same as what is contained in the statement that I gave to the Defence of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to move to a different topic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that statement, is that -- do we have that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not. I tried -- I asked this witness if he can obtain it, and we were not able to obtain the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you try to obtain your statement ^? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we tried to obtain from him. He didn't have it. I don't know what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you make any effort to obtain a copy of that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to my statement, the one that I wrote, I can say the following: I wrote that statement in a single copy. That statement was given to Major Mirko Kosic, who was assistant commander for security and who asked me to write that. Mirko Kosic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is what did you do now to see whether you could receive a copy, because even if it's written only in one copy, then you still can make a copy if it still exists. Did you try to find out whether your statement still is available somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, I didn't know how, except for what I did; that is to say, I asked the lawyer and the members of the team whether they can get that. I personally did not have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you didn't do anything. What did you do apart from asking the witness who then said, "I don't know how to find it. What do you then do, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to consult with my investigators, Your Honours. But maybe we can try it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But isn't that the question that comes, first of all, to your mind if we are talking about a statement taken contemporaneously? I mean, that would be first thing I would immediately go after.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that I asked them to do so, but I don't know exactly what's the progress. Because it's a bit complicated now. It has to go through Sarajevo to reach anything formerly in VRS hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, is the Prosecution in any way in a position to assist?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware of such a statement. We have obviously investigated this matter quite closely, and I will double-check, but I can assure the Chamber that we have not seen a statement from this witness. It didn't come up in our searching either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So even the existence is not confirmed by objective sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 25 of your statement, the penultimate sentence, you say that no one from your brigade ever as much as mentioned that an area in which you were located should be ethnically cleansed, let alone attempted to implement such a thing in practice. Did you have an opportunity to speak to any of the ethnic Muslims in respect of this topic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that you asked first to move into private session at a certain moment, but please tell us exactly when it is that you want us to do that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the command one day and one of the platoon commanders brought a young girl, a Muslim, from the positions and she was in tears, terrified. Of course I took her in, I gave her a bit of encouragement, I let the platoon commander go, and we started talking. During this conversation, she mentioned to me that she had a girlfriend who is an ethnic Serb. It turned out that her friend is a relative of mine. Later on, I'll give the names of both persons. I don't think I should mention them in public now. On that occasion when I asked her what had happened, where she had been, and so on, she said that some unknown people came with some people from their neighbourhood and that they were pressuring the population, the ethnic Croat and Muslim population, telling them that they had to leave their houses because the Chetniks were on their way and that they would slaughter them all. So she and her parents and the rest of the Muslim and Croat population in these neighbourhoods left their houses just with small parcels in their hands, and they fled to the woods and they spent a few days in the woods. However, while they were in the woods some people would return to their homes without having those people who had told them to flee know about that. They went back home to get some things that they needed, and then they returned to the woods. It is then that they transmitted the following piece of news: The people who stayed at home - now, who stayed at home, pregnant women, children, very young children, elderly, frail people - they said that practically nothing had happened, that they were all living at home, normally, and that no one came to their homes. So then she took advantage of such an opportunity as well, fled from the woods, returned to her sister's house. Her sister had a young child at the time. She were there with her sister for a longer period of time. And then, in agreement with this girlfriend of hers, she asked whether it was possible for her to go back home. And the other one said probably. So she tried to get to her home which was somewhere in the area where the units were deployed where otherwise no one was allowed to move about without any ways of being recognised. So by the time she got close to her home, the soldiers captured her and brought her to my office; that is to say, that platoon commander brought her to my office. I treated the girl most fairly. She arrived in tears and she left smiling. Finally, as she was leaving, she added the following, I quote: "Aren't you a good man." Now, I don't want her to get into any kind of trouble on account of all of this, so could we please move into private session so that I can tell you what the girl's name is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Now you told us in closed session how you escorted someone to a safe place with her family. Those people in the school, were they offered also an escort to go to wherever they wanted to go, where their family was living, the women, the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, while I was there, now, I mean, I don't know -- well. Well, what was possible at that time? What was done was seeing off the women and children as safely as possible. Maybe I should explain that completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want you to tell me whether you offered those in the school - women, children - also to go to a place where their family was and where they could be accommodated, with your assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I couldn't do that, if you're referring to me personally. Are you referring to me personally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want to know whether it was done or not, either by you personally or by anyone else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An offer was made to them or, rather, what was done was -- actually, I can just describe the situation. I mean, I don't know that anyone said it as directly as I'm saying it now as we conduct this conversation. But these people - women and children along with this security - they were put onto buses and they went to Vrbanci, taking these buses. Now what happened after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We know that. But when they arrived at the school, did you tell them, If you prefer to go to your aunt or your grandmother or living in one of those villages, please tell us so that we can escort you to bring you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I can say: In the evening when I made this list when I was sitting in that classroom, a woman asked me, What's going to become of us? My answer to her was that I don't know because I'm not the one who is making the decisions on what is going to happen and how things would proceed. So I was not the one who could decide or who could make any offers. At that time, I was in a very low position. I didn't have any authority or any power to say anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You were in the position to have the young girl be accompanied by policemen to return to the place where she thought family was and where she would be safe. So to say that you were in such a low position that you could do -- you couldn't do anything is not really very consistent with what you told us about what you did with the young girl.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. I -- I was in the command there and I had this possibility to get these policemen who were there, part of the command, to do something in particular. But this was a larger group of people. This was in town, whereas this had to do with people who had come to a completely different location, so I could have done that. As far as Grabovica is concerned, that was totally beyond my powers. These people were far away from their homes. Some of them were from -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what time in the evening did you leave the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't leave the school in the evening. I left on the following day in the morning around 10.00, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims remained in the school as well overnight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any mattresses or something to sleep on or did they just sleep on the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, there were no mattresses. There were just school desks because it was a school, after all. Nobody had envisaged that, that that would happen. These people came at night and we had absolutely no possibility. We didn't have any vehicles or anything else to transport these people to some other place where perhaps they could be provided with more decent accommodation. Quite simply, that night in view of the circumstances involved - that is to say, the lack of possibilities that the brigade could offer, the fact that it was night-time, et cetera - they were in these classrooms, they simply sat this way at these desks, they had sort of bent over these desks, and that is how they spent the night. Believe me, we had no other possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So summarising the situation: You took a large number of - apart from the men - a large number of women and children to a place which did not provide proper accommodation, and those were not given a choice either to go to a place where they would have a bed with their families, et cetera. Is that, in short, a part of a description of what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps from your point of view. But viewed from our side, as I told you a moment ago, quite simply, we did not have any other possibilities. That is to say, we did what was possible for us to do at that moment and that is what we offered. But, you know, when you don't have something, you cannot offer that. Secondly, we did not have the capacity, say, to escort each and every woman and child to these villages, Garici, Kotor Varos, these are villages that are far away, Hanifici, or perhaps some other village that they were from. On the other hand, it was most unsafe. Practically this could have meant exposing these people to danger. That would have been a terrible mistake on our part, to try to send these people elsewhere and expose them to that kind of lack of security and safety. I can tell you that already that evening there were a lot of local people who had gathered there and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I do understand that you tell us that you did everything in order to secure their safety and their well-being rather than anything else --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that for that reason they were accommodated in a school where there was no proper accommodation but you had no other choice; and that you, for that reason, did not give them an opportunity to go back to where they came from, from their families. It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It remained a bit unclear because of the English interpretation. Let us go back to the situation when you were speaking to this girl whose name you mentioned in private session. You said that in order for her to go back home, she had to know the password. What does that mean, actually?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it means in practice: When there are combat positions for each and every unit, there are passwords, call-signs, so that people could move about in the zone of combat disposition. If that did not exist, then anybody could walk in, including enemy soldiers, saboteurs, people who would threaten the security of the people who were in these positions. In military practice, that is something that is standard. That is characteristic of all armies in the world. This is not only characteristic of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were these people brought from to Grabovica? Was there any fighting before that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is the following: These people who were in the village of Vecici, now under what circumstances and how this happened, that they set out from Vecici, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any fighting there before that in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were some activates in relation to something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Vecici in the area of replenishment of your brigade or some other brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this term that you used, "replenishment," it is not appropriate. It would be better to say are they in the area of disposition or deployment of the units. Vecici was not in the area of disposition of the Kotor Varos Brigade. That part was covered by a unit from the 22nd Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you went already beyond your 55 minutes you asked for. May I assume that you will finish not later than the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have one more topic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then but -- then at 10.30, I would expect you to more or less have finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. Krsic, let us just look at the last sentence now in paragraph 25. You briefly indicated here that the brigade was multiethnic. What was the ethnic background of the vast majority of the soldiers in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many Muslims and Croats were in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately, say, about 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember now whether there were any komandirs, commanders in your brigade, who were Muslims or Croats? Can you give us a name or some names?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them held the position of komandir. Asim Agan Begovic, he was commander of the logics platoon. Adis Hadziselimovic, who I mentioned a moment ago, he was deputy commander of the platoon of the SPDV; that is to say, the independent anti-sabotage platoon. And Enes Caus, who was deputy commander of a platoon there too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could we have a very accurate and precise time-frame for what the witness tells us at this moment; that is, what situation in time he's describing and whether those who were of Muslim or Croat ethnicity or nationality, whatever you would like to call it, how long they stayed in those positions? The persons you'd just mentioned, they were -- could you -- you've understood my question. Mr. Lukic, if you want to put further questions to the witness on this matter, I leave it in your hands, but that's the kind of information that might assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the question, Mr. Krsic. You heard the question put by Judge Orie. Please answer.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. You asked about these persons of Muslim and Croat ethnicity, when they were in the brigade, from when until when. They were in the brigade from the moment it was established, practically. They became members of the brigade as soon as it was established, and they were members of that brigade until the end of the war; that is to say, throughout the war they remained within that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's true for all, approximately 30, or just for the persons you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It goes for all, all of them. When this first mobilisation of the Territorial Defence took place, they joined. Some of them, for example, the Independent Anti-Sabotage Platoon, it was mobilised at the very outset, and it was multiethnic. Adis Hadziselimovic was deputy commander of that platoon. He was mobilised straight away, and he stayed there until the end of the war. And then also Asim Agan Begovic. As soon as the first mobilisation took place, he joined that unit and he remained in that unit until the end of the war. And I can say that these were exceptionally responsible proper people, fair. As regards the attitude of Serbs towards them, as they were of a different ethnic background, it was most proper. We in the brigade never distinguished among people along those lines, in terms of whether somebody belonged to this or that ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You went well beyond my question, so you emphasized those two persons. And the same is true if the other approximately 28, which makes the group of 30 complete. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No difference whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the witness mentioned a third one as well, Caus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it would be 27. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question before?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the strength of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The strength differed in different periods. I think that in my statements I said that at one point the highest number was between 1.000 and 1500. Sometimes there were less than 1.000, even it went down to 850 men. However, in certain periods, it grew up until 2.000 members. But throughout most of the period of the war, the strength arranged between 1.000 and 1500 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, yes, I can also give you this piece of information: More than 6.000 men passed through the brigade, which meant that the composition of the brigade changed. A very small number of people who were in the brigade at the beginning of the war were actually in the brigade at the end of the war. The personnel changed. More than 6.000 men passed through the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we've stolen a few minutes of your time, so if you want to finish, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krsic, I just wanted to thank you for answering our questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krsic, we'll take a break first and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Krsic. Before I give the opportunity to the Prosecution to cross-examine you, I've one question. You told us about you writing a statement yourself. Are you aware of any statement being taken or written by those who were present when other Muslims have died or any thorough investigation? Do you have any knowledge about such statements or such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mirko Kosic told me that the corps command was requesting statements from those who were present during the events in Grabovica. I personally wrote one. I state that with full responsibility. As for others, I don't know if they also provided statements. And if you permit me, I just wanted to make one comment: Mirko Kosic, who was the assistant commander for security, was one of our best officers among the assistant commanders for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the excellence of persons involved but I'm more focusing on facts. You said you were invited to write a report but you did not -- you were not present when most of the people died which were reported to have been killed. Do I understand that you also do not know whether any reports were written by those who were present when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did at any time someone come back to you and further interview you on the matter? Was there a kind of a thorough investigation, as far as you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mirko Kosic was the only one who requested this of me, and I don't have information about any investigations being conducted later into these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Bibles. You'll find Ms. Bibles to your right. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking just a few initial questions about your background, because there's a few gaps. In paragraph 3, you indicate that you left the JNA on 15 September 1991 on a personal request. You don't describe -- or there is an empty space in your background until July of 1992 when you indicate you went to Kotor Varos, your hometown. What were you doing between September 1991 and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the JNA at my personal request on the 15th of September. So from the 15th of September until the 2nd of July, I was in Zagreb for a period of time. And actually in September, I was in Zagreb. In October, I went to Germany. I spent that time at my sister's in Germany. Then I came back again to Zagreb. I was supposed to continue my PhD studies and I was planning to find a job in Zagreb. Unfortunately, because I was a Serb and a member of the former JNA, I was not able to get a job. The only possibility that was available to me at that time was when my colleague who worked as a driving instructor offered me the option of training and completing traffic school and becoming a driving instructor, and then I could start working at his driving school. From January until June, I attended this traffic school. I completed the fifth degree, fifth level of traffic school, and I became a driving instructor for B category vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. I think that gives us an idea as to what you were doing during this time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could now have 65 ter 31706 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this will be a copy of your appointment to the VRS, or in the VRS, on the 27th of August, 1992. Now, we see that this is signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Dusan Novakovic. Now, this is the same Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic that you discuss in your statement and that you've described as being present in Grabovica during your testimony today; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you initially became, and I think you may have already said this, the assistant chief of staff for operations and training affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then just to sort of jump forward in time, in December of 1992 you eventually become the chief of staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early December. The commander, Dusan Novakovic, informed me of this in early December.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I tender 31706, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31706 receives number P6977, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic was your commanding officer from the moment that you joined in August of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could now go to 65 ter 31376, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You mention a cousin, Zivko Krsic, I believe, in paragraph 20. The document we're going to see is his appointment as the commander for morale and guidance for the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade. Is that the position he held with you joined the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the post I occupied. The document is all right, and the person referred to here did occupy that position. He was the assistant commander for morale guidance. These are two different posts. He was the assistant commander, and I was the assistant chief of staff. These are two different positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I do -- and I apologise if it was confusing. I was talking about your -- this is your cousin; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you refer to him in paragraph 20 of your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And we see that his appointment was dated -- to the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade was dated the 8th of June, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what's stated in the document, that is probably so. I wasn't there in that period, so I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Exactly. And you would confirm that this document, this appointment, is also signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So Novakovic was the commander of this brigade at least from the 8th of June, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when he was appointed the commander of the Kotor Varos Brigade. The information that I have is that I saw the order written by the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps stating that the commander was Slobodan Zupljanin. I came to Kotor Varos on the 22nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, the question -- sir, the question that I asked is if we look at this document, we see that he made an appointment to the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade on the 8th of June, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, in fact, at the time that you joined the brigade there was also a security and intelligence officer, Andjelko Stanic; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andjelko Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting the pronunciation. Would it -- would it surprise you that he was also appointed by Novakovic on the 8th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these men were appointed, if that's what it says, I really cannot comment on it because the information I have does not correspond to what we see in these documents; all the more so because I wasn't there in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Well -- and you've testified to matters about the state of organisation of the brigade when you joined, and that's why we're showing you documents that might show that perhaps your testimony here was mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, before I make a mistake, I would tender 65 ter 31376.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31376 receives number P6978, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bibles, if I may just ask a question before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies. And, Mr. Krsic, at page 29, line 16, you say you came to Kotor Varos on the 22nd of July. By that what do you mean: Kotor Varos, the area; or Kotor Varos, the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I came to Kotor Varos, the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Without going through all of the documents, would you agree that when you arrived at the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, there was a commander for logistics; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't say who --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Nenad Jerkovic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for logistics. It's not Nenad Djokovic but Nenad Jerkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Well, I would certainly accept your pronunciation. But you would agree that he was in that position; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And there was also a chief of the quartermaster service and a chief of medical service when you arrived; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- there was a chief of the quartermaster service and a chief of the medical service, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, if --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could now have P851 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this will be a list of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, at least I believe it's the command staff. And there is no date on this document, sir, and I think you might be able to help us with that. Now, first we see Novakovic at the top, and we see Mane Tepic, and that's your name that's third; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Since your appointment as chief of staff took place in December of 1992, is it correct, then, that this list would have been made sometime between the 27th of August and sometime in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sometime in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So, sir, given the documents that you've seen, isn't it true that, in fact, Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic was the commander of this unit instead of Mane Tepic and that would have been true in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything in relation to these documents. I am saying -- I'm talking about the situation that I found when I came to the brigade. In the period from the 22nd of July until early August, I would go to the command of the Kotor Varos Brigade, and I was told that Mane Tepic was there who was co-ordinating the brigade command; namely, the brigade. At the time, I did not see or had any contact with the commander Dusan Novakovic. Our first contact was on the 28th of August when I came to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified yesterday that the brigade was in complete, I believe the phrase is "disorganisation," when you joined. But will you allow for the possibility that, in fact, there was more organisation than you were aware of before you joined the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not use the term "disorganisation," because that's a more serious term than "unorganised." There is a major difference there. The term that I used, and I explained yesterday what I meant, the brigade was not organised in keeping with military rules. I mentioned the example of the Pioneers Platoon, which should have had 35 men whose speciality was engineering. But out of them there were only five who had that speciality, and the others had different, other specialities. So, in that sense, I was talking about the way the unit was organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll talk in a bit about whether the unit was functioning when you joined. But I want to go back to this list for another reason because you've indicated or you've testified to the ethnicity of the brigade. Sir, as we see on this list --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And we may have to move over a little bit to see it on the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: But this list has a category for ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: This list has a category for ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- in the English translation it says "nationality."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that is correct but --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- just to draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version, sir, up at the top of the category where we see the "Srbin" at the far end of the list, what is that category -- how is that category titled?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, could you speak into the microphone for us? I know you're leaning forward.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an abbreviation, NAC - full stop. It means "nacionalnos," ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. Sir, for brevity purposes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see an "NAC SR." Could the witness also explain what SR means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. At this moment, I don't know myself. Perhaps concluded be socialist republic; SR meaning the socialist republic where the person comes from. This form was used much earlier in the former JNA, so perhaps that's why we have these specific categories.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, in this category we see -- of the names that we can see in the B/C/S version, the word "Srbin", S-r-b-i-n, is present, and that means Serbian; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: For brevity purposes, I'll say that that there are 57 names on this list, and we have to go to the end of the list to see anything other than Srbin or Serbian. We see that everybody on this list is Serbian except for two members.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could now go to page 3 in the B/C/S and page 10 in the English, which is near the bottom of this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We'll see one which is sixth from the top on the B/C/S version -- or sixth from the bottom, I'm sorry, which lists "Yugoslav" as ethnicity; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then moving to page 4 -- excuse me, moving to page 11 in the English and the fourth from the bottom on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We see a blank in this category. Someone who doesn't list a nationality or ethnicity. So, sir, even if these two officers are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we on the right page --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the B/C/S? I'm trying to look for the blank.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Ah, yeah. Yes, if we look fourth from the bottom in the B/C/S, I believe it's been highlighted there, we see a blank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for the assistance of the usher there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, sir, even if these two officers are of non-Serb ethnicity, that's 2 out of 57, which means that 96.5 per cent of the officers for this brigade were Serbian. So, sir, wouldn't you agree that this unit was dominated by Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I agree with you. It's a unit that was predominantly staffed by men who were of Serb ethnicity. I said that in the unit there were about 30 Croats and Muslims. These two that are seen here, Agan Begovic, Asim, and Adis Hadziselimovic are of Muslim ethnicity, but some of them in the earlier period would declare themselves as Yugoslavs. Just as you had a number of Serbs who lived in Croatia who were true Serbs and then when the events started that led to the war in the former Yugoslavia, many of them declared themselves as Yugoslavs or, for example, would say that they did not belong to any particular ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, the question was asked by Mr. Lukic whether the ethnic background of the vast majority -- the witness gave us the numbers. He was talking about 30 on a total of 1.000 up to 1500 or 2.000 which all is in the area of 2, 2-and-a-half per cent. The same is here. So, therefore, you are apparently eliciting evidence on matters which, until now, have been established already in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I apologise, Your Honour. I was showing this document to list the command structure and decided that as long as it was up, we would move -- we'd look at the other features that had been discussed but not shown. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have one question. Sir, you have mentioned one name which is not properly recorded, I think, because I heard the name of an officer Caus or similarly. Can you please tell us, could that man be found on this list? Have you any idea, was he an officer? And can you please spell his name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Enes Caus was assistant commander of the platoon. People who were deputy commanders were not listed here, unless we're talking about independent platoons, like the SPVD or the engineers platoons. He was deputy commander of the platoon and he is not in this list. This list does not mention deputy platoon commanders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who were in other companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he -- he -- his name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to ask you to spell his name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] C-a-u-s. That's his last name. And his first name is E-n-e-s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Can we please move very briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could now move to D428 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, we're shifting more completely to the area of the functioning of units in Kotor Varos and specifically the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade. Sir, this is a -- will be, when it comes up on the screen, a 16 July 1992 order drafted by a Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic, P-e-u-l-i-c, commander of the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade. This is an order, you see, being sent to the 1st Krajina Corps command. Now just for a little bit of background --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And we can go to the last page of this to see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- are you aware that Bosko Peulic --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Whoops, perhaps the second-to-the-last page in the English. My apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- commanded the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade in the 5th Corps of the JNA before the VRS was created?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it the 122nd or the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The 122nd, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when Bosko Peulic was appointed the commander of the brigade. The brigade was the first the 122nd Brigade and then later it was renamed the 22nd Brigade. This date is accurate. As for the rest, it's a fact that he was the commander of the 122nd Infantry Brigade for a period. He was later replaced by Lieutenant-Colonel Janko Trivic. But I don't know when he was appointed commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, that's fine. I just wanted to confirm that he was originally in the JNA and that command followed him to the VRS, and you've actually answered a few questions that were in the future in terms of who took over this brigade. So let's go ahead and look at this document more in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S. We're looking at point number 4 title: "I Have Decided."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We see in the second sentence under "I Have Decided," we read: "Speed up the cleansing," and the B/C/S word is "ciscenje," "of the territory in Kotor Varos municipality and the liquidating of all enemy pockets in the area of responsibility." Now, sir, to be clear, this language is directed against Muslims and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is meant here are enemy forces, organised armed formations from the Muslim and Croat population, made up of that population who were in that area. But this does not refer to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And if we could now go to page 4 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S. We're looking for point 5.3.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: This states that the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade is to carry out and organise combat operations. Now, this is dated the 16th of July, 1992, over a month before you joined. This document shows that Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic relied on the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade to organise and carry out combat tasks; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was that kind of co-ordination between the 22nd Infantry Brigade, the Kotor Varos Brigade, and the Knezeska [phoen] Brigade in that area because the 22nd Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could now go to P4296, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You'll see that this is a 30 June 1992 order regarding command and control of the newly formed brigades in the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P what?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: P -- I'm sorry, 4296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, I can preface this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say the P number again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, P042 -- oh, I'm sorry, 4296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Now it's properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And while this is coming up, sir, I'm showing you this because yesterday at transcript page 29281 you testified that your brigade did not receive orders directly from the 1st Krajina Corps. They came through, and I believe then, it was the 22nd Infantry Brigade. Now, if we could look at point 5 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Which I believe is on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We see the Skender Vakuf and the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigades are resubordinated to the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade. So, sir, isn't it true that since the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade was subordinated to the 122nd, which you said became the 22nd, that the proper flow of orders, in fact, from corps command would have been through the 22nd; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is to say, it was along that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, as opposed to being a communication issue, that's actually proper command and control principles; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with you in that part. There was this other side; namely, that there wasn't developed communication directly between the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and the Kotor Varos Light Brigade. It is correct that this communication evolved to a certain degree -- or to a largest degree, through the commander of the 122nd Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to go to another aspect of your testimony. You testify -- or I believe in 25, and you affirmed it today, that not a single burst or shell was fired on an inhabited place in the zone where your unit was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 2641, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, this is an order from Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic to his subordinate units to carry out an attack dated 24th September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, the 65 ter number was actually 2641. And if we turn to page 4 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S to look at point 5.11. Do we have it on the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, we see that this gives a task for the 82-millimetre Mortar Platoon, and it states: "It will provide support for the 1st and 2nd Light Infantry Companies and the Pioneer Platoon by opening fire on the following areas ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could that portion be enlarged --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Then there's the initials KV. And then it's described as "concentrated fire on the old town, a barrage of fire on the slope east of the Gubavac stream, a barrage of fire on the edge of the forest Lipik and concentrated fire on elevation 334, the village of Duratovic and the village of ...", and I'm going to spell this out, Ravne, R-a-v-n-e. Now, sir, this is an order to part of your brigade to in fact fire shells on inhabited areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order and that is what the order contains. However, what I claim and what I stand by is what I had already stated. The Kotor Varos Brigade never opened fire, including bursts of gun-fire, at populated areas. If these populated areas are listed here, built-up areas, then maybe there should have been open -- maybe there should have been fire at places that are close to these built-up areas, and perhaps there was not topographically a name that could be used for opening this fire. So then the name of the populated area was used as a toponym to indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this specific example, or are you just thinking how it must have been where the text is really talking about, not the fields next to the village but the village. And then to explain to us that it may be that they meant not the village requires at least some specific knowledge about this specific order. Do you have that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have this concrete knowledge and this is what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Ms. Bibles certainly will ask you further about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So, sir, were you involved with the 82-millimetre Mortar Platoon?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That platoon was within our unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you with the mortar platoon when this assault was carried out?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So you don't actually know where the mortars landed or where they were directed as a result of this order?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where the shells were being directed because I was present at the command post; that is to say, the shells were not directed at the populated areas. We have a topographical map in our army, and then according to this topographical map -- it is coded in a certain way, this topographical map in order to replace actual names with some other invented names. And in order to make a topographical map more precise, then certain dots and crosses and other signs are put in, especially in those areas where there would be fire. Since some topographical maps, not all parts of the relief are marked with a toponym --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are telling us in general terms how it happened. I think what we'd like to know: Where you earlier said -- let me just check exactly your words so that I do not -- one second, please. You earlier said: "If these populated areas..." And it escapes from my screen again. One second, please. "If these populated areas are listed here, built-up areas, then maybe there should have been fire ..." Which clearly suggests that you do not know, because you say maybe that is a possibility. Now, tell us exactly what in this order were the coded targets, what military targets were meant here when it said "the village of"? What was it exactly that was supposed to be targeted in this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is planned fire that is referred to; that is to say, that it doesn't mean that this actually did happen. That is one thing. Secondly, hardly ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether it was the fire finally was the result. I asked you what targets are covered, what military targets are covered by the description as we find it in this order. Was it a factory, was it a unit, was it -- because the order says "village," and you are telling us it may not have been the village. If it was not the village, then please tell us what it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are military objectives, the deployment of their units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. You say the village is the deployment of a unit. Do I understand that that unit was in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which unit -- which unit then was it that was attacked at that point in time? What was the formation that you attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I don't know what their formation was, but their positions were discovered in the area of these villages. Usually when we speak, we say "area." So I'm referring to that term. There was no other term, expression, for something that is close to that village and that is why this term was used. And their positions, the forces were near that village. I don't know what the unit was, but these were their objectives, so that is to say that their shelters, foxholes were noted in that area, and then, if necessary, fire was to be opened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not what the document says. You agree with me that it says the village and not unit deployed or the area. It says -- whereas in other respects it's pretty clear that it's talking about elevation number so-and-so, trigger point this and this and this, and here it just says the village, and you are telling us that that was meant to indicate that units deployed not in the village but outside the village were to be targeted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. So units that were around the village, not in the village. Believe me, a populated area was never targeted. None of us in the brigade did that. I mean, really. Really. We were far from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now another question. It also mentioned the concentrated fire on the old town. Is that also meant to be not the old town but troops which were not in the old town? Because the language of the order is fire on the old town. Do you have any explanation as how we would have to understand that as a military target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their forces were deployed in the old town. They were deployed there. That is where they had their fortifications. Their soldiers were deployed there in that position. But the old town is a fortress. It's a fortress, a historical fortress, so it is not a built-up area in the sense of a populated area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you say old town means a fortress in the old town where there was no population left but only troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. This is a very old edifice that was there. It is not a populated area. There are just stone walls there, the remnants of this old historical city. Nearby there wasn't a single house. Absolutely not. There is none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there are any maps or photographs available of Jelsingrad which could confirm this, it would assist the Chamber in -- if it could be produced sooner or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Sorry. You said that the forces were deployed -- the soldiers were deployed in the old town. Is that what you said? It's page 46 from line 9: "Their forces were deployed in the old town." Whose forces were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were the Croat-Muslim armed forces, and this was part of their positions; that is to say, that they had a group of people there. It wasn't a very big group of men in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could now go back, I believe it's page 1 in the English and perhaps page 1 in the B/C/S, to point 2. And if we could enhance page 2, which looks like we're doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, I'll go through the first three lines in the English, describe who's involved and where it's involved, but I'll go on to the objective. Do you see where in point 2 it begins to describe the objective? "With the objective of inflicting the greatest losses on the enemy and manpower and materiel and technical equipment confusing him" -- Excuse me, I was going a little fast. "... and preventing him from engaging in action, and gaining control over all inhabited places in which the enemy has been living." Now, sir, you would agree that these areas would have been inhabited areas, villages, where there would have been civilians as well as soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inhabited places? Yes, civilians were there too. That's correct. However, when it says "place under control," that does not mean carry out a direct attack against these areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, in combination of this with the order of concentrated fire on specific villages, I put it to you that your explanation is trying to make this document into something that it's not.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KRSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I'm trying. That is what is contained in the order, and both you and I can read that. But look, I'm a professional officer, and I can interpret these things in a way in which they were supposed to be interpreted and how this was done to the largest extent. I've already explained this to you, that there is the problem of these reports and these orders. As far as these buildings are concerned, for the sake of precision to determine these points that would be in the focus, and certainly these were not houses directly. These were not populated areas. No one would -- I mean, I've -- myself know that I would never do any such thing, and my other colleagues wouldn't either. So we strictly paid attention to this. If it had to do with the artillery group, then these targets would be around a populated area. There were no direct attacks against populated areas. Efforts were made to take areas around it, dominant features, and when you take that, then you practically place that village under your control. Because, in that case, their forces, their armed forces that are holding these points, they withdraw and, in a way, then that populated area is placed under your control. The essence is that their armed formations should move from that area and that only has to do with armed formations, armed units, and certainly it has nothing to do with the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go to break I would tender 65 ter 2641.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2641 receives number P6979, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Witness, before we take the break, I think you explained in detail about the old town of, I think it was Jelec -- let me see, but you said it was an old fortress and it was far away from any populated area. If you would be provided with a aerial view of that town, would you be able to tell us exactly where that fortress is and so to explain how far that it's away from populated areas? Would you be able to do that, you think?
